title: How I use a Stimulus Processing Performance Model to Help Students Learn Well
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Debbie Thompson, a maths and computer science teacher with more than two decades of experience, describes a simple pipeline she teaches students to diagnose where their learning is stuck: stimulus, processing and performance. She tells them the model is a simplification, but it helps them locate whether the input was too complex, the thinking too shallow or the output too fragile. A computer science example shows her replacing a dense CPU diagram with a recipe analogy so the stimulus was manageable before the vocabulary arrived. An English example shows a colleague changing the processing demand by asking pupils to explain a metaphor to a friend who has not read the poem. On performance, she warns that a correct answer on one day is not evidence of learning and uses spaced retrieval to check retention. She ends with a four-part diagnostic loop.
points: Students can use the stimulus, processing, performance pipeline to name where learning is breaking down, which gives teacher and student a shared language for adapting the lesson.
Changing the stimulus, such as swapping a complex diagram for a familiar recipe analogy, can make a hard topic accessible before technical terms are introduced.
Changing the processing demand, such as asking students to explain a metaphor to someone who has not read the poem, moves them from copying phrases to building understanding.
Good performance on the day can hide shallow processing, so spaced retrieval and varied questions are needed to see whether learning has stuck.
The diagnostic loop checks the stimulus, the processing, the performance and retention over time, and finally transfer to new contexts.
quotes: I tell them to focus on the part of the pipeline process that isn’t working for them, as often difficulties in learning come from one of these three places.

Half the class looked lost because the stimulus was too large a jump for them to make. They could see lots of boxes and arrows, but they weren’t able to make a mental model of what the processor was actually doing in their heads.
By replacing a complex hardware diagram with a familiar everyday process, students were able to begin processing the core idea before dealing with the technical details.
Students underlined phrases and wrote generic comments like: “This shows he is brave.” But Jo realised that they were just copying out phrases rather than analysing them.
Now I’d like you to explain this metaphor to a friend who has never read the poem. What picture should appear in their mind?
Some students can perform well in a test or series of questions on a day, then forget those things the next day.
That shows me that their performance was good but their processing of the method was shallow, and that they need to do more spaced retrieval practice in order to learn.
